subject: Chemistry
title: The Haber Process Feeds the World
description: One-minute skill: The Haber Process Feeds the World.

hook.text: Half the people alive today exist because of one chemical reaction invented in 1909.

buildup.text: Plants need nitrogen to grow, but atmospheric nitrogen (N₂) is almost inert. Crops were running out of fertilizer.

discovery.text: Fritz Haber forced nitrogen and hydrogen to combine under high pressure and heat, producing ammonia.

twist.text: Haber also developed chemical weapons used in WWI. His wife, a chemist, shot herself in protest.

climax.text: The Haber process now produces 150 million tons of ammonia yearly. It feeds 4 billion people.

punchline.text: One reaction feeds half the world. Its inventor also made poison gas.

quiz.question: What does the Haber process produce?

details.summary: The Haber process converts atmospheric nitrogen and hydrogen into ammonia under high pressure and temperature using an iron catalyst. This reaction enabled synthetic fertilizer production and now supports roughly half the world's food supply through enhanced crop yields.
details.whyItMatters: Without the Haber process, Earth could sustain only about four billion people. It is arguably the most consequential chemical reaction in human history for its impact on global food security.
takeaways: The Haber process fixes nitrogen gas into usable ammonia
It supports food production for roughly half of humanity
The reaction requires extreme pressure and an iron catalyst

faq.question: Why was the Haber process considered so revolutionary when it was invented?
faq.answer: Before 1909, usable nitrogen came only from natural deposits and biological fixation, both limited in scale. The Haber process unlocked the atmosphere's vast nitrogen reserves for agriculture, averting predicted mass famines in the twentieth century.

faq.question: What are the environmental downsides of the Haber process?
faq.answer: The process consumes roughly two percent of global energy and produces significant carbon dioxide emissions. Excess ammonia fertilizer also causes waterway eutrophication and nitrous oxide emissions, a potent greenhouse gas.
